memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text: "Esau held a grudge against Jacob because of the blessing his father had given him. He said to himself, 'The days of mourning for my father are near; then I will kill my brother Jacob.'" - Gen 27:41 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
Esau's grief now curdles into something darker. He "held a grudge" against Jacob and began plotting murder in his heart: "then I will kill my brother." What began as a genuine hurt has grown, unchecked, into deadly hatred.

This is how bitterness works. A real wound — and Esau's was real; he had been genuinely wronged — can, if we nurse it, harden into hatred. Bitterness rarely stays still. Left to grow, it poisons the heart and reaches for revenge. The Bible warns us to guard against any "bitter root" that springs up and causes trouble (Heb 12:15).

The tragedy is that Esau had cause for grief, yet grief was never meant to become murder. We cannot always control being hurt, but we can decide what we do with the hurt. Will we bring it to God and let Him heal it, or will we feed it until it consumes us?

Jesus went to the very root of this when He warned that anger and hatred in the heart are themselves deadly (Matt 5:21-22). The remedy is not to deny our pain but to release it — to forgive as we have been forgiven (Eph 4:31-32). Do not let a wound become a grudge, or a grudge become a poison. Bring your hurt to the God who heals.

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
1. Is there a wound I am nursing that is turning into bitterness?
2. What do I do with my hurts — bring them to God or feed them?
3. Whom do I need to forgive before a grudge takes deeper root?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text: Lord, search my heart for any bitter root. Help me to bring my hurts to You for healing and to forgive others as You have forgiven me. Amen.
